description: Traceable quantitative baselines for HumanityAI problem categories. These indicators describe important dimensions of problems; they are not priority scores.

records.name: People living in extreme poverty under the World Bank international poverty line

source.title: March 2026 global poverty update from the World Bank: New data and updated poverty numbers

limitations: This is an estimated global count, not a direct census of people in poverty.
The $3.00/day international poverty line uses 2021 purchasing-power parities and is intended for global comparability; national poverty lines are generally more appropriate for country-level policy.
Monetary poverty does not capture all dimensions of material insecurity or human capability.
records.notes: The World Bank's March 2026 update estimates 847 million people in extreme poverty in 2024 and nowcasts a global extreme-poverty rate of 10.0% for 2026.

records.name: People not fully covered by essential health services
limitations: The estimate reflects coverage of essential health services and is not a direct measure of health outcomes, quality of care, or all unmet medical need.
Underlying global health indicators have reporting lags and heterogeneous national data quality.
This indicator should not be added to financial-hardship counts because the affected populations overlap.
records.notes: WHO reports that the UHC service coverage index rose from 54 in 2000 to 71 in 2023, while about 4.6 billion people remained not fully covered in 2023.

records.name: People without access to electricity

source.title: World Energy Outlook 2025 — Achieving access for all

limitations: Electricity access is a threshold measure and does not by itself capture reliability, affordability, generation quality, or sufficient power for productive use.
The global estimate can conceal large geographic and socioeconomic disparities.
records.notes: IEA reports roughly 730 million people without electricity and notes that progress remains insufficient for universal access on current trends.

records.name: People lacking access to clean cooking

source.title: World Energy Outlook 2025 — Achieving access for all

limitations: The rounded global count does not capture differences in exposure intensity, household fuel stacking, affordability, or reliability of clean cooking options.
Health impacts from polluting cooking depend on exposure and context, so this count should not be treated as a direct morbidity estimate.
records.notes: IEA reports around 2 billion people lacking clean cooking access; this connects essential infrastructure with health and economic opportunity.

records.name: States with active armed conflicts

source.title: SIPRI Yearbook 2026 — Global trends in armed conflict

limitations: A count of states with active conflict does not measure conflict intensity, fatalities, duration, geographic extent, or the number of people affected.
Conflict classification depends on definitional thresholds and can change when conflicts cross borders or involve actors with disputed status.
This indicator should not be interpreted as a direct measure of the probability that any individual experiences violence.
records.notes: SIPRI reports armed conflict active in 49 states in 2025, with most conflicts remaining internal while interstate armed conflicts increased relative to 2024.

records.name: People forcibly displaced worldwide

source.publisher: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees
source.title: Global Trends 2025

limitations: Forced displacement includes heterogeneous populations and causes, including conflict, persecution, violence, human-rights violations, and events seriously disturbing public order.
The total combines categories with different legal statuses and data-generation methods and should not be treated as a count of unique harms beyond displacement itself.
A decline in the stock of displaced people can reflect returns under difficult conditions and is not automatically evidence that underlying conflicts or rights conditions improved.
records.notes: UNHCR reports 117.8 million forcibly displaced people at the end of 2025, down from 123.2 million at the end of 2024.

records.name: People lacking access to secure, safe, and adequate housing

source.title: World Cities Report 2026: The Global Housing Crisis — Pathways to Action

limitations: UN-Habitat reports this as an 'up to' estimate, reflecting substantial uncertainty in global measurement and definitions of housing inadequacy.
Housing inadequacy covers multiple overlapping dimensions such as insecurity of tenure, overcrowding, affordability, informality, environmental hazards, and inadequate services.
This figure should not be summed with homelessness, slum-population, or displacement estimates because those groups substantially overlap.
records.notes: The 2026 World Cities Report states that up to 3.4 billion people lack access to secure, safe, and adequate housing, including more than 1 billion people in informal settlements and slums.

records.name: Children and youth out of school

source.title: 2026 GEM Report — Access and equity: countdown to 2030

limitations: Out-of-school status measures enrollment/access rather than learning quality, attendance consistency, completion, or skills acquired.
Global estimates depend on population projections and incomplete reporting; conflict-affected settings can be systematically undercounted.
Age-group composition matters because barriers and intervention options differ substantially between primary, lower-secondary, and upper-secondary ages.
records.notes: UNESCO reports 273 million children and youth out of school in 2024 and notes that the global out-of-school population has risen for seven consecutive years.

records.name: Global average surface temperature anomaly above the 1850–1900 average

source.title: WMO confirms 2025 was one of warmest years on record

limitations: WMO reports an uncertainty margin of plus or minus 0.13 degrees Celsius around the consolidated estimate.
A single global annual temperature anomaly does not capture regional extremes, ocean heat, precipitation shifts, sea-level rise, ecosystem effects, or human exposure.
An individual year's anomaly is influenced by natural variability and should be interpreted within the long-term warming trend.
records.notes: WMO's consolidated analysis of eight datasets estimated 2025 at 1.44°C above the 1850–1900 average and confirmed the past 11 years as the 11 warmest on record.

records.name: Global prevalence of self-reported loneliness

source.title: From loneliness to social connection: charting a path to healthier societies — Report of the WHO Commission on Social Connection

limitations: Loneliness is subjective and measured with heterogeneous survey instruments, sampling frames, and cultural interpretations across countries.
The 15.8% figure is a pooled estimate across evidence collected between 2014 and 2023, not a point-in-time census for 2025 or 2026.
Loneliness and objective social isolation are related but distinct constructs and should not be treated as interchangeable.
records.notes: The WHO Commission on Social Connection estimates that approximately one in six people globally report loneliness, with higher prevalence among adolescents, young adults, and people in lower-income countries.

records.name: Countries classified by the World Bank as having high within-country inequality
records.reference_period: 2022 classification using most recent available household survey for each country

source.title: Inside the World Bank’s new inequality indicator: The number of countries with high inequality

limitations: The World Bank classifies a country as highly unequal when its income-or-consumption Gini index exceeds 40; this threshold is a policy indicator rather than a natural dividing line.
Country Gini measures are based on household surveys that differ in reference concept and timing; the World Bank harmonizes them for comparability but residual differences remain.
Data recency is a major limitation: for 2022, 51 countries had Gini estimates based on household surveys more than five years old.
A country count weights countries equally regardless of population and does not measure global interpersonal inequality, wealth inequality, or unequal access to non-income opportunities.
records.notes: Using the World Bank Poverty and Inequality Platform, the World Bank identified 52 countries with Gini index above 40 in 2022, down from 77 in 2000. This is retained as one dimension of P09 rather than a complete inequality score.

records.name: People in the global jobs gap
limitations: This is a projection for 2026, not a direct census or final observed value.

The jobs gap measures people who want paid work but cannot access it; it does not measure job quality, earnings adequacy, bargaining power, productivity, underemployment intensity, or whether work expands human capability.
The measure combines different forms of labour-market exclusion, so subgroup composition matters for diagnosis and intervention choice.
Unemployed people are included within the broader jobs gap, so this figure must not be added to unemployment counts.
records.notes: ILO projects the global jobs gap—the broader group of people who want paid work but cannot access it—to reach 408 million in 2026, compared with projected unemployment of about 186 million (4.9%). This is one dimension of P07, not a complete economic-opportunity score.

records.name: People remaining offline from the Internet

source.title: Measuring digital development: Facts and Figures 2025

limitations: Internet use is a threshold access/use measure and does not capture connection quality, affordability, digital skills, meaningful use, censorship, accessibility, device ownership, or whether connectivity expands human capability.

ITU estimates are revised as newer country data become available; the 2024 online/offline estimates were revised in the 2025 edition, so historical comparisons should use a consistent vintage when possible.
A global count conceals large income, gender, age, and urban-rural divides; ITU reports 94% Internet use in high-income countries versus 23% in low-income countries in 2025.
Being offline is only one dimension of unequal access to science, innovation, and technology and should not be treated as a complete P13 measure.
records.notes: ITU estimates that 6.0 billion people, or 74% of the world's population, used the Internet in 2025 while 2.2 billion remained offline. This is retained as an access baseline for P13 rather than as a claim about the quality or social value of connectivity.
